newsitem.title: GERMANY: US team to visit Kigali ahead of rescue mission.
newsitem.headline: US team to visit Kigali ahead of rescue mission.

text.p: U.S. military officials in Germany geared up on Thursday for a projected deployment of troops to Africa to help refugees in Zaire as an American observation team visited the troubled region.

A 37-strong military group headed for the Rwandan capital Kigali on Thursday after spending Wednesday night in Uganda, U.S. Air Force Major Bryan Holt of the U.S. European Command said. Some officials are expected to go on to Zaire.

The team arrived in central Africa on the same day President Bill Clinton tentatively agreed to order a few thousand U.S. troops to Africa for an aid and rescue mission, which the White House said it expected to last about four months.
The observation team has been sent to Africa to investigate how to send American troops into the region.
"They do not have a set itinerary and they will stay however long it takes to plan for this mission," Holt said.
The U.S. European Command, based in Stuttgart, is responsible for U.S. military operations in Europe, some areas of the Middle East and most of Africa, including Zaire.
"We have not gotten any additional orders yet," Holt said. But he added, "We are in the planning phase and are tailoring plans to any specific mission that we are given."
About 1,000 U.S. ground troops are expected to be sent to eastern Zaire to help desperate Rwandan and Burundian Hutus, some cut off from help since local Tutsis rebelled a month ago.
The first troops, including about 600 elite paratroopers from the U.S. 508th Airborne Infantry Regiment based at Vicenza, Italy, could leave for Africa as early as next week.
A further 2,000 to 3,000 American troops would go to nearby countries to help with support activities, the Pentagon said.

The United States has painful memories of a U.N. relief mission to Somalia in 1993, which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other foreign troops. Many were sent from U.S. bases in Germany and may return to Africa for the Zaire mission.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters on Wednesday the United States planned to send about 1,000 troops to the eastern Zaire town of Goma to secure and run the airport, the key centre for distributing relief.
They will also set up a protected corridor about two miles (three km) long from Goma to nearby Rwanda to allow refugees to return to Rwanda if they voluntarily choose to go, the Pentagon said.

Defence officials said other U.S. troops in the task force were expected to include air cargo handlers and medical, civil affairs and "psychological operations" personnel, who would encourage refugees to voluntarily return to Rwanda.
Canadian, British and French troops are also expected to take part in the mission.
U.S. officials said the multinational force would be under the overall command of a Canadian general, but the U.S. forces would serve directly under an American general who will be deputy commander.

The world community, under pressure to react to the crisis, is anxious to avoid a re-run of 1994 when it effectively fed and gave sanctuary to many of those responsible for the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Rwandans, mainly Tutsis.

Then hundreds of thousands of Hutus poured into eastern Zaire fearing reprisals by victorious Tutsi rebels for the genocide launched by the Hutu-led army and militia groups, but supported by large sections of the population.

Many camps were run by the same Hutu killers, many local mayors and regional leaders, who then used them as bases from which to launch a comeback, infuriating the new Tutsi-led government in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
